steps.title: In It for the Long Haul

blocks.markdown:
Ever know an individual who tried to fight every battle? Maybe you’re thinking of someone in your office right now. You may even be thinking of yourself! As a woman, there are a few strategic principles to staying in it for the long haul and making your career go the distance when others before you have flamed out.

Become a Go-To Team Player
The first is, become a go-to team member. Remember the previous lesson about being your authentic self? Don’t wait for recognition or a promotion to become an ideal team player. As a coach, Pat intentionally looked for players who wanted the ball—those who had declared themselves competitors and felt confident enough in their skills to request the ball when the game was on the line. Their team knew they could count on them to perform so they became the go-to. This takes intentionality and sometimes going above and beyond in strategic areas. The key word is strategic. Learn how to best add value to your team without automatically accepting every assignment that comes your way.

You can’t fight every battle. You just cannot. When it comes to women in the workplace overall, and your career specifically, know which battles to fight and which to leave alone. Grow your long-term perspective. This has several advantages as you progress as a female leader.

sections.title: Strategic Decision-Making
sections.body: Knowing when to pick your battles involves assessing the importance of an issue, understanding the potential impact on your career, and considering the long-term consequences of engaging in a particular issue.

sections.title: Preserving Energy and Focus
sections.body: Engaging in every battle can be exhausting and detract from your overall focus and productivity. Knowing when to pick your battles allows you to preserve your energy for the issues that truly matter.

sections.title: Demonstrating Emotional Intelligence
sections.body: Emotional intelligence plays a big role in workplace dynamics. Choosing battles requires recognizing and managing emotions effectively, leading to more constructive interactions between you and your peers.

sections.title: Distinguishing Between Major and Minor Issues
sections.body: Not every workplace issue requires the same level of your attention. Period. Major issues that align with your core values or significantly impact your work should be prioritized.

sections.title: Assessing the Long-Term Impact
sections.body: Consider the long-term impact of a potential conflict. Will the issue at hand have lasting consequences on your career, relationships, or the overall work environment?

sections.title: Evaluating Personal Investment
sections.body: If the matter directly affects your responsibilities, well-being, or professional growth, it may be worth addressing. However, for issues that are more peripheral to your role, choosing to step back might be the wiser option.

questions.prompt: How can you become a go-to player?

choices.text: Learn how to add value to your team.
Stay late every evening at work.

questions.prompt: Which is not an important part of picking your battles?

choices.text: It ensures you get a raise faster.
